briefs.learning_objective: Recognize that a spreadsheet is a grid of cells addressed by column letter and row number, and that a workbook can contain multiple named sheets.

required_facts.statement: A spreadsheet's cells are grouped into rows and columns, forming a grid, and each cell can contain a number, text, or a formula.

Cells are referenced by their location in the row and column on the sheet, for example cell A1 is in the first row of column A; by default, Excel uses the A1 reference style, referring to columns with letters and rows with numbers, so a cell like B2 is at the intersection of column B and row 2.
A workbook can contain multiple sheets, often called spreadsheets, and you can add as many sheets to a workbook as you want.
By default, Excel names worksheets Sheet1, Sheet2, Sheet3 and so on; the name appears on the sheet tab and can be renamed.

briefs.learning_objective: Write a single-cell reference and a range reference in A1 notation, including a whole-row or whole-column range.

required_facts.statement: A reference identifies a cell or a range of cells on a worksheet, and tells Excel where to look for the values you want to use in a formula.
In the A1 reference style, a cell is referred to by its column letter followed by its row number, for example B2.
A10:A20 refers to the range of cells in column A and rows 10 through 20; A10:E20 refers to the range in columns A through E and rows 10 through 20.
An entire row or column can be referenced with just its row number or column letter repeated on either side of a colon, for example 5:5 for all cells in row 5, or H:H for all cells in column H.

briefs.learning_objective: Convert a data range into an Excel table, and reference the table's columns with structured references instead of raw cell ranges.

required_facts.statement: To quickly create a table from a data range, select the cell or range and then select Home > Format as Table, and pick a table style.
By default, a table has a header row that labels each column, and the header row can be turned off if not wanted.
source_refs: excel_tables_overview#Learn about the elements of an Excel table

required_facts.statement: The combination of table and column names used in a formula instead of explicit cell references is called a structured reference; for example, instead of =SUM(C2:C7), a formula can use =SUM(DeptSales[Sales Amount]).
Typing a value in a cell just below a table's last row, or in a cell to the right of its last column, expands the table to include that new row or column.

briefs.learning_objective: Define a name for a cell or range, and use that name inside a formula instead of the range's raw cell address.

required_facts.statement: To name a cell or range, select it, type a name into the Name Box, and press Enter.
Once a name is defined, typing the name into a formula, or selecting Formulas > Use in Formula and choosing the name, lets that formula reference the named cell or range instead of its raw address.

optional_enrichment.statement: Using names makes formulas easier to understand and maintain, and Excel's Name Manager (Formulas > Name Manager) lets you create, edit, delete, and find all the names used in a workbook.
source_refs: excel_named_ranges_guide#Manage names in your workbook with Name Manager

briefs.learning_objective: Sort a data range by one column, and sort by more than one column with an independent direction chosen for each.

required_facts.statement: To sort a column of numbers, select a cell in that column and, on the Data tab in the Sort & Filter group, select Sort Smallest to Largest or Sort Largest to Smallest.
To sort a column of dates or times, select a cell in that column and select Sort Oldest to Newest or Sort Newest to Oldest.

To sort by more than one column, open the Sort dialog box from Data > Sort, choose the first column to sort by in the Sort by box, then select Add Level to add another column to sort by; entries higher in the list are sorted before entries lower in the list.
source_refs: excel_sort_data_guide#Sort by more than one column or row

required_facts.statement: Each level added in the Sort dialog box has its own Order setting, so different columns within the same multi-level sort can be sorted in different directions.
source_refs: excel_sort_data_guide#Sort by more than one column or row

briefs.learning_objective: Apply AutoFilter to a data range using a numeric comparison on one column together with a value match on another column, so only rows meeting all conditions are shown.

required_facts.statement: To filter a range of data, select any cell within the range, select Data > Filter, select the column header's filter arrow, choose Number Filters or Text Filters and a comparison such as Greater Than, enter the filter criteria, and select OK.
AutoFilter shows the data you want and hides the rest; clearing a filter redisplays all of the data.
source_refs: excel_filter_data_guide#Filter data in a range or table in Excel

required_facts.statement: A range or table can be filtered by more than one column at once; filters are additive, so each additional filter is based on the current filter and further reduces the subset of data shown.
source_refs: excel_filter_data_guide#Filter data in a range or table in Excel

briefs.learning_objective: Apply a conditional formatting rule that automatically formats cells meeting a threshold condition.

required_facts.statement: Conditional formatting applies a format to cells automatically based on rules you create that determine the format based on the cells' values.
source_refs: excel_conditional_formatting_guide#Use conditional formatting to highlight information in Excel

required_facts.statement: To apply a quick conditional formatting rule, select the cells, then on the Home tab in the Style group select Conditional Formatting > Highlight Cells Rules, choose a comparison command such as Less Than, enter the comparison value, and select a format.
source_refs: excel_conditional_formatting_guide#Format cells that contain text, number, or date or time values

briefs.learning_objective: Restrict a cell or range to only accept values from a fixed list by adding a dropdown-list data validation rule.

required_facts.statement: Data validation restricts the type of data or the values users can enter into a cell, such as a dropdown list, and can display a customized error message when a user enters invalid data.

To add a dropdown-list data validation rule, select the cells, select Data > Data Validation, on the Settings tab set Allow to List, then in the Source box type the list values separated by commas, making sure the In-cell dropdown check box is selected.
source_refs: excel_data_validation_guide#Add data validation to a cell or a range

required_facts.statement: Data validation can also restrict entry to a whole number, decimal, date, time, or text length within limits: under Allow choose the type (for example Whole Number), under Data choose a condition (for example between), and then enter the minimum, maximum, or specific value to allow.
source_refs: excel_data_validation_guide#Adding other types of data validation

briefs.learning_objective: Remove duplicate rows from a data range using the Remove Duplicates tool, choosing which columns define a duplicate.

required_facts.statement: When you use the Remove Duplicates feature, the duplicate data is permanently deleted, so it's a good idea to copy the original data to another worksheet before removing duplicates.

To remove duplicates, select the range of cells that has duplicate values, select Data > Remove Duplicates, and then check or uncheck the columns under Columns to choose which columns are used to identify a duplicate row.

briefs.learning_objective: Split one column of delimited text into separate columns using the Convert Text to Columns Wizard.

required_facts.statement: To split text into columns, select the cell or column that contains the text, select Data > Text to Columns, choose Delimited, select the delimiter(s) such as Comma or Space, choose the destination for the split data, and select Finish.

briefs.learning_objective: Write a formula on one sheet that references a cell on a different sheet in the same workbook.

required_facts.statement: A formula can refer to a cell on another sheet in the same workbook by writing the sheet name followed by an exclamation point (!) and then the cell or range reference, for example Marketing!B1.
source_refs: excel_formulas_overview#Making a reference to a cell or a range of cells on another worksheet in the same workbook

required_facts.statement: If the referenced worksheet's name contains spaces or numbers, the name must be enclosed in single quotation marks in the reference, for example ='January Revenue'!A1.
source_refs: excel_formulas_overview#Making a reference to a cell or a range of cells on another worksheet in the same workbook

required_facts.statement: A workbook link (previously called an external reference) to a cell range in another workbook, when the source workbook is open, includes the workbook name in square brackets, followed by the worksheet name, an exclamation point, and the cells the formula depends on, for example =SUM([Budget.xlsx]Annual!C10:C25).
source_refs: excel_workbook_links_guide#What a workbook link to another workbook looks like

briefs.learning_objective: Write a formula that begins with an equal sign and combines cell references and arithmetic operators, or a built-in function, into one computed value.

required_facts.statement: Formulas in Excel always begin with the equal sign (=).
source_refs: excel_formulas_overview#Create a formula that refers to values in other cells

required_facts.statement: Excel's arithmetic operators include + for addition, - for subtraction, * for multiplication, and / for division; for example =2+4, =4-2, =2*4, and =4/2 are all valid formulas.

To enter a formula that contains a built-in function, type an equal sign and the function's name, an opening parenthesis, then select the range of cells the function should use, and a closing parenthesis, then press Enter.
source_refs: excel_formulas_overview#Enter a formula that contains a built-in function

required_facts.statement: To create a formula that refers to values in other cells, select a cell, type an equal sign, select or type the first cell's address, enter an operator such as - for subtraction, select or type the next cell's address, and press Enter.
source_refs: excel_formulas_overview#Create a formula that refers to values in other cells

required_facts.statement: Excel performs the operations in a formula in a specific precedence order (for example, multiplication and division before addition and subtraction); parentheses change that order — =5+2*3 gives 11, but =(5+2)*3 gives 21.

briefs.learning_objective: Distinguish a relative cell reference from an absolute cell reference, and use $ notation to keep a reference fixed when a formula is copied.

required_facts.statement: A relative cell reference, such as A1, is based on the relative position of the cell containing the formula and the cell it refers to; if you copy or fill the formula across rows or down columns, the reference automatically adjusts, and by default new formulas use relative references.
source_refs: excel_formulas_overview#The difference between absolute, relative, and mixed references

required_facts.statement: An absolute cell reference, such as $A$1, always refers to a cell in a specific location; if you copy or fill the formula across rows or down columns, the absolute reference does not adjust.
source_refs: excel_formulas_overview#The difference between absolute, relative, and mixed references

required_facts.statement: A mixed reference has either an absolute column and relative row (for example $A1) or an absolute row and relative column (for example A$1); when the formula is copied, the relative part adjusts and the absolute part does not.
source_refs: excel_formulas_overview#The difference between absolute, relative, and mixed references

briefs.learning_objective: Use SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, and COUNTA to summarize a range of values into a single number.

required_facts.statement: The SUM function adds values; its syntax is SUM(number1, [number2], ...), where each argument can be a number, a cell reference, or a range, for example =SUM(A2:A10).

The AVERAGE function returns the average (arithmetic mean) of its arguments; its syntax is AVERAGE(number1, [number2], ...), and if a range or cell-reference argument contains text, logical values, or empty cells, those values are ignored, though cells with the value zero are included.

The COUNT function counts the number of cells that contain numbers; its syntax is COUNT(value1, [value2], ...), and only numbers in the array or reference are counted, while empty cells, logical values, text, and error values are not.

The COUNTA function counts the number of cells that are not empty in a range, counting cells with any type of information including text and error values, but not empty cells; its syntax is COUNTA(value1, [value2], ...).

briefs.learning_objective: Write an IF formula, including nested IFs, and combine conditions with AND or OR to build the logical test.

required_facts.statement: The IF function tests a condition and returns one value if the condition is TRUE and another value if it's FALSE; its syntax is IF(logical_test, value_if_true, [value_if_false]).
Multiple IF functions can be nested inside each other in order to perform more than one comparison.

The AND function returns TRUE if all of its arguments evaluate to TRUE, and returns FALSE if one or more arguments evaluate to FALSE; its syntax is AND(logical1, [logical2], ...), and it is commonly used as the logical_test argument of IF to test more than one condition at once.
The OR function returns TRUE if any of its arguments evaluate to TRUE, and returns FALSE if all of its arguments evaluate to FALSE; its syntax is OR(logical1, [logical2], ...).
Text in formulas goes in quotes; for example =IF(A2>B2,"Over Budget","OK") tests whether A2 is greater than B2 and returns one of the two quoted text results.
A nested IF can convert a numeric score to a letter grade, for example =IF(D2>89,"A",IF(D2>79,"B",IF(D2>69,"C",IF(D2>59,"D","F")))).

briefs.learning_objective: Combine several text values into one string using TEXTJOIN or CONCATENATE, inserting a delimiter between the joined values.

required_facts.statement: TEXTJOIN combines text from multiple ranges or strings and inserts a delimiter you specify between each text value; its syntax is TEXTJOIN(delimiter, ignore_empty, text1, [text2], ...).
In TEXTJOIN, setting the ignore_empty argument to TRUE skips empty cells among the arguments rather than joining them in as blank values.

CONCATENATE joins two or more text strings into one string; its syntax is CONCATENATE(text1, [text2], ...), though Microsoft recommends using the newer CONCAT function instead, since CONCATENATE may not be available in future versions of Excel.

briefs.learning_objective: Extract a substring from fixed positions in a text value using LEFT, RIGHT, or MID, and remove extra spaces using TRIM.

required_facts.statement: LEFT returns the first character or characters in a text string, based on the number of characters you specify; its syntax is LEFT(text, [num_chars]).
RIGHT returns the last character or characters in a text string, based on the number of characters you specify; its syntax is RIGHT(text, [num_chars]).
MID returns a specific number of characters from a text string, starting at the position you specify; its syntax is MID(text, start_num, num_chars).
TRIM removes all spaces from a text value except for single spaces between words; its syntax is TRIM(text).

briefs.learning_objective: Compute a date-based value, such as an age in years, using TODAY together with DATEDIF.

required_facts.statement: The TODAY function returns the serial number of the current date and takes no arguments; its syntax is TODAY().

The DATEDIF function returns the difference between a start_date and an end_date in the unit you specify; its syntax is DATEDIF(start_date, end_date, unit), where a unit of "Y" returns the number of complete years in the period.
DATEDIF is useful in formulas where you need to calculate an age.
Excel stores dates as sequential serial numbers so they can be used in calculations; by default, January 1, 1900 is serial number 1.
DATEDIF's unit argument "D" returns the number of days in the period between start_date and end_date.

briefs.learning_objective: Aggregate only the rows that match one or more conditions using COUNTIF, COUNTIFS, SUMIF, or SUMIFS.

required_facts.statement: COUNTIF counts the number of cells in a range that meet a single criterion; its syntax is COUNTIF(range, criteria).

COUNTIFS applies criteria to cells across multiple ranges and counts the number of times all the criteria are met together; its syntax is COUNTIFS(criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2], ...), and each additional range must have the same number of rows and columns as criteria_range1.

SUMIF sums the values in a range that meet criteria you specify, optionally applying the criteria to one range while summing the corresponding values in a different range; its syntax is SUMIF(range, criteria, [sum_range]).

SUMIFS adds the cells in a sum_range that meet multiple criteria at once, where each criteria_range/criteria pair is a separate condition that must all be met; its syntax is SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2], ...).

Criteria for these functions can be a number, expression, cell reference, or text, such as 32, ">32", B4, or "apples"; criteria containing comparison symbols or text must be enclosed in quotation marks.
The same range can be used in more than one criteria pair to test a range condition, for example =COUNTIFS(A2:A7,"<6",A2:A7,">1") counts values between 1 and 6.

briefs.learning_objective: Write a VLOOKUP or XLOOKUP formula that finds a key in a table and returns a corresponding value from another column.

required_facts.statement: VLOOKUP looks up a value in the leftmost column of a range and returns a value from the same row in a column you specify by its position; its syntax is VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, [range_lookup]).

In VLOOKUP, entering FALSE (or 0) for range_lookup searches for an exact match to lookup_value; leaving range_lookup blank or entering TRUE searches for an approximate match instead, and TRUE is the default if the argument is omitted.

HLOOKUP works like VLOOKUP but searches across the top row of a table and returns a value from a row you specify by its position; its syntax is HLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, row_index_num, [range_lookup]).

XLOOKUP searches lookup_array for lookup_value and returns the corresponding item from return_array, producing an exact match by default; its syntax is XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode]).
VLOOKUP can only look up a value from left to right, but XLOOKUP works in any direction and returns exact matches by default.
source_refs: excel_vlookup_index_match_guide#Using INDEX and MATCH instead of VLOOKUP

briefs.learning_objective: Combine INDEX and MATCH to look up a value when the return column is not to the right of the key column.

required_facts.statement: MATCH searches for a specified item in a range of cells and returns the relative position of that item within the range; its syntax is MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_array, [match_type]).

Setting MATCH's match_type to 0 finds an exact match; a match_type of 1, or omitting the argument, finds the largest value that is less than or equal to lookup_value, and requires lookup_array to be sorted in ascending order.
INDEX returns the value of an element in a range or array, selected by its row and column position; the array form's syntax is INDEX(array, row_num, [column_num]).

VLOOKUP can only look up a value from left to right, meaning the column containing the lookup value must be to the left of the column containing the return value; when the layout isn't built that way, MATCH can find the row position of the key and INDEX can then return the value from any column at that row position.
source_refs: excel_vlookup_index_match_guide#Using INDEX and MATCH instead of VLOOKUP

briefs.learning_objective: Given a formula's error value, diagnose which class of problem — a failed lookup, an invalid reference, or a wrong data type — is causing it.

required_facts.statement: The #N/A error generally indicates that a formula can't find what it's been asked to look for; the most common cause is with XLOOKUP, VLOOKUP, HLOOKUP, LOOKUP, or MATCH functions when the lookup value doesn't exist in the source data.
The #REF! error shows when a formula refers to a cell that's not valid, which happens most often when cells that were referenced by formulas get deleted or pasted over.
#VALUE! is Excel's way of saying there's something wrong with the way a formula is typed, or something wrong with the cells it's referencing.

A formula like =A1+B1+C1 can break and return a #VALUE! error if any of the referenced cells contains a non-numeric (text) value, whereas a SUM formula over the same cells ignores the text values and sums only the numeric ones.
If AVERAGE or SUM refer to cells that contain #VALUE! errors, the formulas will result in a #VALUE! error.

briefs.learning_objective: Build a PivotTable that places one field in Rows, another in Columns, and a numeric field in Values.

required_facts.statement: A PivotTable is a tool to calculate, summarize, and analyze data that lets you see comparisons, patterns, and trends in your data.
source_refs: excel_pivottable_guide#Create a PivotTable to analyze worksheet data

required_facts.statement: To create a PivotTable, select the data cells, select Insert > PivotTable, choose where to place the PivotTable report, and select OK.
source_refs: excel_pivottable_guide#Create a PivotTable in Excel for Windows

required_facts.statement: To add a field to the PivotTable, select its checkbox in the PivotTable Fields pane; selected fields are added to their default areas, with non-numeric fields added to Rows and numeric fields added to Values, and a field can be moved to a different area by dragging it there.

Filters area fields are shown as top-level report filters above the PivotTable; Columns area fields are shown as Column Labels at the top of the PivotTable; Rows area fields are shown as Row Labels on the left side of the PivotTable; Values area fields are shown as summarized numeric values in the PivotTable.

briefs.learning_objective: Change a PivotTable value field's summary function, recognizing that Sum is the default for numeric fields.

required_facts.statement: Data in a PivotTable's Values area summarizes the underlying source data by default using the SUM function for numeric values and the COUNT function for text values.
source_refs: excel_pivottable_summary_guide#Change the summary function or custom calculation for a field in a PivotTable

required_facts.statement: To change a value field's summary function, select the field in the Values area, on the PivotTable Analyze tab select Active Field > Field Settings (or right-click the value and choose Value Field Settings), select the Summarize Values By tab, and choose the summary function you want, such as Average.

briefs.learning_objective: Build a bar chart from a summary table, arranging category and value data in columns or rows before inserting the chart.

required_facts.statement: Bar charts illustrate comparisons among individual items; in a bar chart, the categories are typically organized along one axis and the values along the other.

To create a chart, select the data for the chart, select Insert > Recommended Charts, and select a chart on the Recommended Charts tab to preview it; if you don't see a bar chart you like, select the All Charts tab to see all chart types, select the chart, and select OK.
source_refs: excel_create_chart_guide#Create a chart from start to finish

briefs.learning_objective: Build a line chart from time-ordered data to show a trend across the sequence.

required_facts.statement: In a line chart, category data is distributed evenly along the horizontal axis and value data along the vertical axis; line charts can show continuous data over time on an evenly scaled axis, making them well suited to showing trends at equal intervals such as months, quarters, or fiscal years.

To create a chart, select the data for the chart, select Insert > Recommended Charts, and select a chart on the Recommended Charts tab to preview it; if you don't see a line chart you like, select the All Charts tab to see all chart types, select the chart, and select OK.
source_refs: excel_create_chart_guide#Create a chart from start to finish

briefs.learning_objective: Build a pie chart that shows each category's share of a single total.

required_facts.statement: Pie charts show the size of items in one data series proportional to the sum of the items, and are appropriate when you have only one data series to plot, none of the values are negative, there are no more than seven categories, and the categories represent parts of the whole pie.

To create a chart, select the data for the chart, select Insert > Recommended Charts, and select a chart on the Recommended Charts tab to preview it; if you don't see a pie chart you like, select the All Charts tab to see all chart types, select the chart, and select OK.
source_refs: excel_create_chart_guide#Create a chart from start to finish

briefs.learning_objective: Given a description of an experiment, identify its control group, its treatment group, and the metric being compared between them.

required_facts.statement: Studies where researchers assign treatments to cases are called experiments; when the assignment includes randomization, it is called a randomized experiment.
Researchers randomly assign cases to a control group and a treatment group so that differences between the groups that cannot otherwise be controlled are evened out.

A/B testing works by showing two variants of a page or experience to users at random: the original (control, or A) and a modified version (variation, or B); engagement with each version is measured and then compared against the baseline, the control.

briefs.learning_objective: Compute and interpret the lift (percentage change) between a treatment group's result and a control group's result.

required_facts.statement: Relative improvement (lift) is the percentage difference in the variation's conversion rate over the baseline (control) conversion rate; for example, a 10% relative improvement over a 25% baseline conversion rate means the variation's conversion rate is 27.5%.
Relative improvement describes the variation's change as a percentage of the baseline's rate.
Analyzing an A/B test's results means determining whether the variation had a positive, negative, or neutral effect compared with the baseline (control).

briefs.learning_objective: Given two results with the same estimate but different sample sizes, explain why the estimate from the larger sample is more trustworthy.

required_facts.statement: A bigger sample tends to provide a more precise point estimate than a smaller sample.

The more cases researchers observe, the more accurately they can estimate the effect of the explanatory variable on the response; in a single study, this is done by collecting a sufficiently large sample.

optional_enrichment.statement: When talking about the variability of a point estimate, such as a sample proportion, the term standard error is typically used rather than standard deviation.

briefs.learning_objective: Given a result reported with a significance or confidence figure, explain what that figure does and doesn't tell you about the underlying effect.

required_facts.statement: The null hypothesis (H0) often represents a skeptical position or a perspective of "no difference", and the alternative hypothesis (HA) represents an alternative claim under consideration.

The p-value is the probability of observing data at least as favorable to the alternative hypothesis as our current data set, if the null hypothesis were true; it is used to quantify the strength of evidence against the null hypothesis.

Statistical significance is a measure of how unusual an experiment's results would be if there were actually no difference in performance between the variation and the baseline and the discrepancy were due to random chance alone.

A confidence interval represents a range of plausible values where we are likely to find the population parameter; if many samples were taken and a 95% confidence interval were built from each one, about 95% of those intervals would contain the parameter.

Describing a confidence interval as capturing the population parameter with a certain probability is a common error; while it may be useful to think of it that way, the confidence level only quantifies how plausible it is that the parameter is in the given interval.

When the sample size becomes large, even a very small, practically unimportant difference can be detected and called statistically significant; such a difference is statistically significant but not practically significant.

misconceptions.statement: Not every confidence interval captures the true population proportion: in an illustrative set of twenty-five 95% confidence intervals built from different samples (around p = 0.88), only one failed to contain the population proportion, showing that a small fraction of intervals will miss it even when the method is followed correctly.

briefs.learning_objective: Given an experiment's results, state a business conclusion that follows from the data without overreaching beyond what the numbers show.

required_facts.statement: The null hypothesis (H0) often represents a skeptical perspective or a claim to be tested, and the alternative hypothesis (HA) represents an alternative claim under consideration; the value being compared to the parameter in this setup is called the null value.

In one hypothesis-test example, because the null value (p0 = 0.333) fell within the confidence interval computed from the sample, that value was not implausible, so the data did not provide sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis.

In a second example, the null value (p0 = 0.333) was not in the 95% confidence interval, so the null hypothesis was rejected: the data provided statistically significant evidence that the proportion differed from 0.333, and because the entire interval was below 0.333, it was concluded to be lower.
Analyzing an A/B test's results means determining whether the variation had a positive, negative, or neutral effect compared with the baseline (control).

When the sample size becomes large, even a very small, practically unimportant difference can be detected and called statistically significant; for example, an online experiment might find that placing additional ads on a movie review website statistically significantly increases viewership of a TV show by 0.001%, but this increase might not have any practical value.

While we failed to reject the null hypothesis in the first example, that does not necessarily mean the null hypothesis is true; perhaps there was an actual difference, but we were not able to detect it with the relatively small sample of 50.

misconceptions.statement: Failing to reject the null hypothesis is not equivalent to accepting the null hypothesis as true; it only means there was not strong enough evidence for the alternative.
